archetype.name: Better Than Its Record
archetype.definition: A Detroit team that is controlling play at 5-on-5 better than it has in years but is being sunk by bad finishing, a broken penalty kill and an uneven crease, so its 4-4-3 understates how it is actually playing.

report.headline: Out-shooting, out-chancing, and still losing: Detroit's record lags well behind its play.
report.take:
On the standings page this looks like the same Red Wings as the last five years: a .500-ish record, a negative goal differential, a site rank of 24th, tied for the Atlantic basement with Buffalo. Underneath, it is a different team. Detroit owns 53.3% of the expected goals at 5-on-5 (10th) and 54% of the shot attempts (7th), and it is putting 29.9 shots on goal a game (6th) while allowing 24.7 (10th). For context, the best xGF % this franchise posted in any of the last five seasons was .488 last year, and its CF % never got above .49. Eleven games is a small sample, but a jump from a perennial possession underdog to a top-ten possession team is the most important thing on this sheet.

So why 4-4-3? Three leaks. First, the finishing: the skaters are shooting 8.5% in all situations, 29th in the league and nearly three points under the league average, which is why a team generating that much volume ranks 26th in goals a game. Dylan Larkin has one goal on 28 shots; Seider has none on 20. Second, the penalty kill is at 65.8%, 30th, more than twelve points below the league's average, turning every penalty into a coin flip. Third, the goaltending is split: John Gibson has taken most of the starts with an .867 save % and -4.2 GSAx, while Daniil Tarasov has stopped .940 with +5.1 GSAx in three starts. Add a run of one-goal and overtime games, and a team that played well enough to be above .500 is instead sitting on 11 points.

What the numbers hide is that the offense is narrow. DeBrincat (12 points, +7), Raymond (9 points, six on the power play) and the rookie-age wing Brandsegg-Nygård (+10, a .644 xGF %) are driving it, with Finnie quietly productive at center. Behind them, Copp is playing 18 minutes a night with three points and a .445 xGF %, Rasmussen has three points, and Kolesar has none. The forward and blueline groups both grade C, and the goaltending grade is a D because of Gibson's start, not Tarasov's.

The direction is encouraging: 3-1-1 over the last five, outscoring opponents 15-14 after a rough opening stretch. Shooting percentage at this depth almost always climbs back toward league average, and if the penalty kill merely becomes bad rather than historic, this team's results should start to match its process. The open question is whether the 5-on-5 dominance is a new reality or an 11-game mirage; history says be careful, the shot share says believe a good part of it.

strengths.title: Owning the puck at 5-on-5
strengths.body: Detroit is winning the shot-attempt and expected-goal battles by clear margins, a sharp break from five straight seasons below 49% in both. It shows up in raw volume too: they are among the league's top shooting teams and suppress shots better than most. Possession numbers stabilize faster than goal totals, so even with an 11-game sample this is the most trustworthy part of the profile.

strengths.title: A top line that produces
strengths.body: DeBrincat and Raymond are both top-11 wingers on the site's tabs, and Brandsegg-Nygård is posting a .644 xGF % with a +10 in 15 minutes a night. DeBrincat has six goals on 42 shots, a finishing rate that is real for a shooter of his type rather than a fluke. This trio is why the power play is at league average despite the team's overall shooting slump.

strengths.title: Tarasov has been excellent
strengths.body: In three starts Daniil Tarasov has a .940 save %, a 1.40 GAA and +5.1 GSAx, the 8th-ranked goalie on the site. That alone has pulled the team's GSAx back to slightly above league average despite Gibson's struggles. It is too small a sample to call him the answer, but it is a reason to give him more of the net.

concerns.title: A penalty kill in free fall
concerns.body: At 65.8%, the kill is 30th in the league and far below the league average, and it is the single biggest reason a team allowing so few shots still gives up a middling number of goals. Detroit was at 70.1% two seasons ago, so this has been a recurring weakness rather than pure bad luck. Some regression upward is likely, but it is unlikely to become an asset.

concerns.title: Finishing well below the league
concerns.body: An 8.5% shooting rate on all those shots is the main reason the offense ranks 26th in goals a game. Larkin's one goal on 28 shots and Seider's zero on 20 are the clearest examples. This should improve on its own, but the bottom of the lineup is not creating much either, so not all of it is luck.

concerns.title: Gibson's start and thin depth
concerns.body: Gibson has an .867 save % and -4.2 GSAx across most of the starts, dragging the goaltending grade to a D. Meanwhile Copp is logging heavy minutes with a .445 xGF % and Kolesar has no points, so the depth lines are giving back what the top line builds. If the crease and the middle six don't change, the good possession numbers may keep translating into mediocre results.

trend.note: After a rough start that included a loss to Seattle at home and two straight overtime losses, Detroit has gone 3-1-1 over its last five and turned a positive goal differential in that stretch, a 0.7 points % that is well above its season mark.

weekAhead.headline: Oilers' power play and a Florida back-to-back bracket two home gifts
weekAhead.body:
The week opens in Edmonton against an 8-2-1 team whose record is built on the league's best shooting percentage and the top Pts vs Goal Diff, not on controlling play: the Oilers are under 50% in xGF % and CF %, and their goalies are last in GSAx. Detroit should carry the 5-on-5 play there, but Edmonton's 35.1% power play against a 30th-ranked kill is exactly the matchup that has been costing the Wings games. Staying out of the box is the whole game plan.

Then come two home games that are as soft as the schedule gets. Chicago is 31st on the site, below 41% in both shot share stats, with a dead-last power play and a defense giving up points to forwards and defensemen well above expectation. St. Louis is a .500 team that has been leaking points to centers, which is a chance for Larkin and Finnie to break through. The week closes with a road back-to-back in Florida: the Panthers allow only 22.2 shots a game, third-fewest, and Tampa grades A- at forward and on the blueline with a top-five xGF %. Both Florida teams have shaky goaltending, so Detroit's volume could finally cash in, but the second night of a back-to-back on the road against Tampa is the toughest spot of the week.

keyMatchups.title: Oilers power play vs Detroit's kill
keyMatchups.body: Edmonton converts 35.1% of its power plays, second in the league, and Detroit kills only 65.8%. Edmonton's 105.1 all-situations PDO suggests it is riding hot finishing, but special teams can decide the game before regression ever arrives. Discipline is the swing factor in the opener.

keyMatchups.title: Chicago is a slump-buster
keyMatchups.body: The Blackhawks hold just 40.3% of expected goals and allow forwards 1.25 points a game above expectation, 30th in the league. If Detroit's shooters are going to regress upward, this is the game. Anything less than a comfortable win would be a red flag about the finishing.

keyMatchups.title: Florida back-to-back, shots at a premium
keyMatchups.body: Florida suppresses shots as well as almost anyone, and Tampa's skater groups are among the league's best. Both, though, have goalies saving well below the league average, so Detroit's shot volume can still matter. Splitting these two would be a good result.

weekAhead.watch: Who starts in goal, and how often: if Tarasov gets the Edmonton and Tampa starts, the club is telling you the crease has changed.

restOfSeason.body:
The 82-point pace is the floor, not the forecast. A team that controls play like this rarely keeps shooting 8.5% for long, and the penalty kill has room to climb back toward the 70s it has posted in recent seasons. If those two things normalize, Detroit should score closer to the league average and play something like .530 to .560 hockey the rest of the way, which lands it around the 85-to-93 point range it has lived in for three seasons, with upside if the 5-on-5 gains are real. The caution is the history: five years of sub-49% shot shares say some of this early dominance will fade, and the depth forwards and Gibson's start limit how high the ceiling is.

What will regress: the shooting percentage (up), the penalty kill (up, but only partly), and Tarasov's .940 (down). What looks sustainable: the top line's production and a shot share that, even with some fade, should stay around 50% or better. In an Atlantic where Boston, Tampa and Ottawa are already pulling away, that likely puts Detroit in the bubble conversation rather than comfortably in.
swingFactors: Tarasov vs Gibson in the crease
Whether the 5-on-5 shot share holds near 53%
Penalty kill recovering toward league average

confidence.note: Eleven games; the possession jump contradicts five seasons of history.
